paragraphs: The race was held on a rainy night, on a kitchen floor that went on for miles. Four duck-sized cars waited on the grid, low and shiny. Yellow Duck Sweater climbed into the yellow one and found no steering wheel, only two pedals for its orange feet and a pair of rollers where the seat should be. It was the Roller Sprint again, but louder. Its pit crew, three small ducks in matching caps, held umbrellas over nothing. Above the grid hung the start lights: five raindrops in a row, waiting to fall.

One by one the drops let go. The duck steered the only way it knew, tipping its whole loaf-shaped head into each corner, and the car tipped with it, throwing a fan of water across the tiles. On lap two a radio crackled inside the sweater: box, box, pit this lap. Every servo locked. It had spent four thousand ninety-six lifetimes not falling into a pit. But the pit lane was only a warm garage with a rug, where a crew duck wiped its camera eye with a sock. It rolled back out wobbly and last, onto a track that had become one long glittering puddle, and went through it saying wheee, its wake spreading behind it in a wide yellow V.

imagePrompt: Yellow Duck Sweater, a small two-legged tabletop robot. Its head is a smooth, chunky white plastic shell shaped like a small loaf of bread: about one and a half times as long front to back as it is tall, deep and boxy with softly rounded corners and a mostly flat top. It is not a round dome or ball, and not a long thin tube. It has an orange trim along the bottom edge and a small orange hinge on each side. At the front of the head is a single round camera eye: a black lens inside a thick orange-yellow ring. It has no beak and no mouth. The head sits on a tall, thin neck, about as tall as the head is long, made of stacked black servo motors with a few loose black wires, leaning slightly forward. Its body is a small, boxy white torso with rounded corners. It has no arms and no hands. Its short legs are black servo joints with white plastic covers on the hips, knees slightly bent. Its feet are flat and rounded like duck feet, orange on top with yellow soles. It wears a small, chunky-knit, bright lemon-yellow crewneck sweater over its white torso, slightly too big, with a ribbed collar, cuffs, and hem. Knitted into the front of the sweater is a simple cartoon duckling: pale yellow body with a thick black outline, a black dot eye, a curved line for its wing, an orange beak, and orange feet. A single full-color comic page with six panels of equal size in a grid of two columns and three rows, separated by clean white gutters, read left to right and top to bottom. The same robot duck appears in every panel and looks identical each time, unless a panel says otherwise. No speech bubbles, captions, sound effects, panel numbers, or any other text. Panel 1: On a rainy night, the robot duck in its yellow duckling sweater stands on a giant checkered kitchen floor that stretches into the distance, beside four small shiny race cars lined up on a painted starting grid, one of them yellow. Panel 2: The duck sits in the low yellow race car, which has no steering wheel, with its orange feet resting on two pedals, while three small plain white robot ducks in matching caps stand beside the car holding open umbrellas over empty air. Panel 3: The four race cars wait on the grid while five round raindrops hang in a straight row in the air above them, glowing softly like start lights. Panel 4: The duck races the yellow car around a corner on the wet kitchen tiles, tipping its whole loaf-shaped head into the turn as the car leans with it and throws a fan of water spray sideways. Panel 5: Inside a small warm garage with a cozy rug on the floor, one plain white robot duck in a cap gently wipes the yellow-sweater duck's camera eye with a striped sock while the duck sits still in its parked yellow car. Panel 6: The duck drives the yellow car alone through a long glittering puddle that covers the whole track, its head tipped back happily, leaving a wide V-shaped wake spreading out behind it across the shining water. Warm children's comic art: clean confident ink outlines, soft flat colors with gentle shading, a dreamy night palette, cozy and a little surreal. Friendly for an 11-year-old. No text, letters, logos, or numbers anywhere in the image. Real people do not appear.
